post.description: A `table` trigger is installed in the branch's database by the worker (`pending_install`, then `installed` or `failed`); each committed matching row change is then POSTed to the function's `fetch` handler with header `chelabase-event: db` and body `{id, type, schema, table, record, old_record, txid}` (over 256 KiB: `record` and `old_record` null, `truncated: true` and `primary_key`). Delivery is at least once (dedupe on `id`): a non-2xx answer is retried with backoff, and the 10th failure makes the event dead (`dead_count`). Events queue while the function is disabled; a pending event is never dropped, and dead events past 10,000 per database or 7 days are removed and counted (`dropped_count`). The database's compute stays awake while it has an installed table trigger. A `table` trigger is installed, and stays installed, only while the function's run-as role on the branch (the role identity approved when run-as was set) has table-level `SELECT` on the table and, when the table has row level security enabled, has `BYPASSRLS` or owns the table without `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`; a row change is queued only while that holds. Otherwise the trigger is uninstalled, its queued events are dropped (`dropped_count`) and it settles `failed` with `last_error` `run_as_role_required` (no run-as role), `run_as_role_cannot_read_table` (the role is gone or lacks `SELECT`) or `run_as_role_subject_to_rls`; after fixing the cause, turn the trigger off and on. post.description: Renders the operations to SQL (names quoted, expressions as given, each exactly one SQL expression) and runs them on one of the branch's Postgres databases as the owner (Admin only) or, with `role`, as that role (the SQL editor's session: your member role, then `SET ROLE`), in one transaction with `lock_timeout` (`lock_timeout_ms`, default 5000) and `statement_timeout` (60 s; 15 s for a dry run). A dry run runs the same statements and always rolls back; it evaluates your expressions (defaults, checks, `USING`), so their non-transactional side effects (e.g. `nextval`) remain. A statement that may rewrite a table over `CHELABASE_TABLE_API_DRY_RUN_MAX_BYTES` (default 256 MiB), and every one after it, is only rendered in a dry run (`skipped`), and then `would_succeed` is null. A table the request names that doesn't exist (and no earlier operation creates) is 404 with its `op_index`. Drops end `RESTRICT` and a request with drops returns `dependents`: what `CASCADE` would also remove beyond the request's own drop targets and their parts, and their `hash`. When something depends on a drop and the request confirms no cascade, the dry run and the real run alike answer 409 `has_dependents` with `dependents`, and change nothing. To cascade, send that hash as `cascade.dependents_hash`: the run (dry or real) locks the drop targets' tables, reads the dependents again, and refuses with 409 `dependents_changed` when they differ or when Postgres reports dropping anything but them and the parts of the request's other drop targets (drops that reach each other, e.g. a parent table and its child, need the hash of no dependents); a drop whose target an earlier drop of the request already removed is `skipped` (`already_dropped`). A `CONCURRENTLY` index operation must be the request's only operation: it runs outside a transaction (`statement_timeout` 900 s; a dry run only checks it), can't cascade, and when its build fails after creating its index, that INVALID index is dropped (another index of the same name never is). Postgres errors keep their fields (`op_index`, `sqlstate`, `message`, `detail`, `hint`, `position`; `dry_run: true` on a dry run). Each request is logged with its operation count, never its SQL.

A real run is destructive when any operation carries one, adds a foreign key whose `on_delete` or `on_update` is anything but `no_action` or `restrict`, drops something, changes a privilege, owner, schema, policy or row-level security, changes a column's type, default or identity or lifts NOT NULL, or isn't known; otherwise write.

post.description: Runs a script on one of the branch's Postgres databases on a fresh connection as the database's owner (Admin only), or, with `role`, as that role: the connection logs in as your own hidden member role on the branch, which can only become the roles you were granted (and what they can become), then runs `SET ROLE` to `role`, so a script that resets its role is never the owner. When the run ends (however it ends), its session is ended, whatever the script made as the member role itself is handed to `role`, and every privilege, default privilege or policy naming the member role is dropped. An Admin acting as a role a member role can't hold (LOGIN, owner-level, or reaching a reserved role) uses the owner's connection and `SET ROLE`; naming the owner runs as the owner. Without `read_only`, the script is sent unchanged as one simple query, so multi-statement scripts, explicit transactions and commands like `VACUUM` work. With `read_only: true`, every statement runs inside one transaction Postgres holds read-only (begun `READ ONLY`, its snapshot taken first, rolled back at the end, the connection never reused): Postgres refuses any write, including one made by a function a `SELECT` calls, and any switch back to read-write, in that session only (an extension that opens its own connection, such as `dblink` or a foreign-data wrapper, is outside the guarantee). Only `SELECT` (with `WITH`, `VALUES`, `TABLE`), `SHOW` and `EXPLAIN` may appear at the top level, at most 100 statements; any other statement (transaction control, `SET`, `RESET`, `DISCARD`, `COPY`, `DO`, `CALL`, `LOCK`, ...) or a script that doesn't parse refuses the whole script with 422 `read_only_script_refused` before anything runs. Each statement is prepared on the server before it runs, and the first error ends the run (a statement whose command tag isn't a read's also ends it, with `25006`). A read-only run's timeout is at most 300000 and `confirm` can't be sent with it. Unless `confirm` is true (and the run isn't read-only), risky statements (drops, truncates, `DELETE`/`UPDATE` without `WHERE`, also under `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` or `PREPARE`, and anything that doesn't parse) and, on a protected branch, every statement that isn't a read are held back with 409 `sql_confirm_required`. Errors before the connection opens are JSON; then the answer is `200 application/x-ndjson`, one JSON event per line: `notice`, `columns` (`statement`, `columns: [{name, type}]`), `rows` (`statement`, at most 200 rows of text-or-null values), `complete` (`statement`, `tag`, `rows`, `truncated`: over 1,000 rows), `error` (`statement`, `code`, `message`, `detail`, `hint`, `position`: 1-based in the sent text; in a read-only run, in its statement), `heartbeat` (after 15 s without another event) and, always last, `done` (`outcome`: `ok`, `error`, `cancelled`, `timeout` or `truncated_response` past 10 MiB; `duration_ms`). Closing the stream cancels the run. Every run is logged with its command tags and a SHA-256 of the script, never the script.

Nothing on the target is undone: `result.leftovers` lists what the merge left there that the online phase didn't finish, each `{kind, schema, table, name}`: `not_valid_constraint` (a constraint added `NOT VALID`, never validated; it still checks new rows); `not_null_check` (a temporary `chelabase_merge_nn_*` check that wasn't dropped); `invalid_index` (the index the online phase was building, or dropping concurrently, when it stopped: Postgres may have left it INVALID, unused by queries but still updated by writes; it may also not be there); `unattached_index` (a valid index the merge built that its next step didn't put into place: a temporary `chelabase_merge_ix_*` index not renamed over the one it replaces, or a unique constraint's index not attached to its constraint; nothing uses it, and it costs on every write). post.description: Refuses, in this order: a merge that isn't `rehearsed` (`merge_not_rehearsed`, or `merge_stale` for a stale one); a `version` that isn't the merge's (`merge_version_conflict`: a save of acknowledgements or the after-merge choice keeps a merge rehearsed, so send the version you last saw to apply what you saw); conflicts without a resolution (`merge_conflicts_open`); data-loss, security (BYPASSRLS, owner-level) or breaking (a role rename) steps without an acknowledgement (`merge_drops_unacknowledged`); a protected target without `confirm: true` (`merge_confirm_required`); another merge applying to the target, or failed half applied on it (`merge_busy`). A plan with a security step or user SQL (a `user` step, or `own_sql` from a resolution; steps run as the branch's owner) is applied only by an Admin, on any target. The worker then runs the plan (`applying`, then `online` for the concurrent index and validation steps, then `finishing`). The request doesn't read the target: before the plan's transaction the worker compares the target with the schema the plan was computed from, and if it changed, ends the merge `stale` without applying the transaction.

The grant is checked on every member's union of sources narrowed by their overrides, on every database of the project, as `putProjectGrant` checks one grant; a refusal names the member, the team and the database.
